enriched_description: Large North American true frog measuring 9-15 cm in snout-vent length (up to 20 cm total). Body is robust and broad-headed with smooth, moist skin exhibiting variable coloration from olive-green to brown dorsally with irregular dark mottling; ventral surface is white to yellowish with grey mottling. Most distinctive feature is the large tympanum (eardrum) visible as a circular membrane behind the eye; in males, the tympanum is significantly larger than the eye, while in females it is approximately equal to eye diameter. Eyes are large, golden-brown, and protruding, positioned dorsolaterally on the head. Hind limbs are extremely long and muscular with fully webbed feet adapted for powerful swimming leaps; webbing extends to the tips of all toes. Forelimbs are shorter with unwebbed digits. Males exhibit a yellow throat during breeding season. The frog exhibits a characteristic semi-aquatic posture, floating with only eyes and nostrils exposed or basking on banks with body low to ground.

Small arboreal frog measuring 2-7 cm in snout-vent length with slender body and smooth, moist skin. Most distinctive feature is the presence of enlarged adhesive toe pads (suckers) on the tips of all digits, enabling climbing on vertical surfaces and smooth leaves; toe pads are circular, flattened, and slightly concave with a sticky mucous coating. Skin coloration is typically bright green (providing camouflage among foliage) but varies by species to include brown, yellow, or patterned forms. Some species exhibit lateral stripes or dorsal markings. Eyes are large and protruding with golden or copper irises. Hind limbs are long with partial webbing between toes; forelimbs are slender. The frog exhibits a characteristic perching posture on leaves and branches with limbs splayed and toe pads adhering to the surface. Skin texture is smooth and slightly granular. Many species have a white or cream ventral surface.

Small western North American frog measuring 3-5 cm in snout-vent length with compact, toad-like body and rough, granular skin. Body coloration is dark brown to black with mottled patterning providing camouflage against rocky stream beds. Skin is rough and warty with small tubercles distributed across the dorsal surface. Head is broad and flattened with small, protruding eyes positioned dorsolaterally. Most distinctive feature is the male's tail-like copulatory organ (post-anal appendage), a unique structure among frogs, used for internal fertilization in fast-flowing streams. Hind limbs are moderately long with partially webbed feet; toes lack adhesive pads. Forelimbs are short and stout. The frog exhibits a characteristic clinging posture on submerged rocks in fast-flowing mountain streams, using its rough skin and body shape to resist current. No external tympanum is visible. Ventral surface is pale grey to white.

Large sea turtle measuring 70-100 cm in carapace length and weighing 80-200 kg. Carapace (upper shell) is heart-shaped when viewed from above, reddish-brown to dark brown in coloration with a smooth, glossy surface composed of large, non-overlapping scutes (horny plates). The carapace has five vertebral scutes down the midline and four pairs of costal scutes on each side. Plastron (lower shell) is cream to yellowish with a smooth surface. Head is large and broad with a massive, hooked beak adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey (crabs, mollusks). Eyes are small and dark. Front flippers are long and paddle-like with a single claw on each; rear flippers are shorter and used for steering. Skin is scaly and grey-brown on exposed surfaces. The turtle exhibits a characteristic swimming posture with front flippers providing powerful, wing-like propulsion through the water. No ability to retract head into shell.

Largest living turtle measuring 120-180 cm in carapace length and weighing 250-700 kg. Most distinctive feature is the carapace, which lacks the hard bony scutes of other sea turtles; instead, it is covered in thick, leathery, oily skin with seven longitudinal ridges (keels) running from head to tail. Carapace coloration is dark grey to black with scattered white or pale spots. Plastron is similarly leathery with five longitudinal ridges. Head is large with a distinctive notched upper jaw creating a double-pointed appearance. Eyes are small and dark. Front flippers are extremely long and narrow relative to body size, proportionally the longest of any sea turtle, enabling sustained oceanic migration. Rear flippers are short. Skin is dark grey with a smooth, rubbery texture. The turtle exhibits a characteristic open-ocean swimming posture with continuous, powerful flipper strokes. Can dive to depths exceeding 1,200 meters. No ability to retract head into shell.

Small freshwater turtle measuring 8-14 cm in carapace length with a high-domed, oval carapace that is dark brown to black with a smooth, slightly glossy surface. Carapace has three longitudinal keels (ridges) in juveniles that become less prominent with age. Plastron is small and yellowish with two hinges allowing partial closure. Head is relatively large with a pointed snout and small eyes positioned laterally. Skin is grey to brown with a rough, scaly texture. Limbs are short and stout with webbed feet and sharp claws adapted for digging in muddy substrates. Tail is short and thick. The turtle exhibits a characteristic bottom-walking posture in shallow, muddy waters, often partially buried in sediment with only eyes and nostrils exposed. Can emit a strong musky odor from glands when disturbed. No ability to fully retract into shell due to small plastron.

Medium-sized freshwater to brackish water turtle measuring 12-25 cm in carapace length. Carapace is oval and moderately domed with a smooth surface; coloration varies from brown to olive with concentric growth rings visible on each scute. Some species exhibit ornate patterning with yellow or orange markings on dark scutes. Plastron is large and hinged, enabling partial closure. Head is moderately sized with a pointed snout and small eyes; skin coloration is grey to olive with distinctive striped or spotted patterning on the head and neck. Limbs are moderately long with webbed feet and sharp claws. Tail is short. The turtle exhibits a characteristic basking posture on logs or banks with limbs extended and head raised. Skin texture is smooth with fine scales. Adapted for both aquatic and terrestrial environments, spending significant time basking to regulate body temperature.

Medium-sized terrestrial turtle measuring 12-20 cm in carapace length with a high-domed, oval carapace. Most distinctive feature is the hinged plastron (lower shell) that can close completely against the carapace, fully enclosing the turtle for protection; the hinge is located transversely across the midline of the plastron. Carapace coloration is dark brown to black with variable yellow, orange, or radiating markings on each scute creating a distinctive pattern. Surface texture is smooth with concentric growth rings. Plastron is yellow to brown with dark markings. Head is moderately sized with a pointed snout and small eyes; skin coloration is brown to grey with orange, yellow, or red markings on the head, neck, and limbs. Limbs are stout and elephantine (columnar) with non-webbed feet and curved claws adapted for terrestrial locomotion. Tail is short. The turtle exhibits a slow, deliberate walking gait on land. Skin texture is rough and scaly.

Small gecko measuring 7-14 cm in total length with slender body and distinctive dark transverse bands across the back. Body coloration is pale grey, pink, or cream with 4-6 broad, dark brown to black bands running from the neck to the tail base; bands are sharply demarcated and evenly spaced. Skin is smooth and granular with fine, bead-like scales. Most distinctive feature among geckos is the presence of movable eyelids (unlike most geckos which have a fixed transparent spectacle). Eyes are large with vertical slit pupils adapted for nocturnal vision. Tail is cylindrical and slightly flattened, capable of autotomy (self-amputation) when threatened; regenerated tail is smooth and lacks banding. Limbs are slender with five digits; toes lack the adhesive lamellae (setae) of typical geckos, reflecting a terrestrial rather than climbing lifestyle. Digits have small claws. The gecko exhibits a characteristic nocturnal foraging posture with body low to the ground and head raised.

Large tropical lizard measuring 120-200 cm in total length (including tail) with robust body and distinctive dorsal crest. Most prominent feature is the row of enlarged, spine-like scales running from the nape of the neck along the midline of the back to the tail base, forming a serrated crest; crest spines are most prominent in males. Body coloration is bright green in juveniles, becoming darker green to greyish-green in adults with broad black bands on the body and tail. Skin is covered in small, granular scales with larger, plate-like scales on the head. Head is large and triangular with a prominent dewlap (loose skin fold) hanging from the throat; dewlap is enlarged in males and used in display. Eyes are large with round pupils and golden irises. A large circular subtympanic shield (scale) is present below the tympanum. Limbs are long and muscular with five clawed digits on each foot; digits are long and adapted for climbing. Tail is laterally compressed and longer than body, used for balance and defense. The iguana exhibits an arboreal posture with body horizontal on branches and limbs splayed.
